(a) Increase in Number of Judges.—Subsection (a) of section 7443 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (relating to the number of judges on the Tax Court) is amended by striking out “16” and inserting in lieu thereof “19”.
 
    (b) 
Removal of Age Limitation.—Subsection (b) of section 7443 of such Code (relating to appointment to the Tax Court) is amended by striking out the last sentence.
 
    (c) Effective Date.—The amendments made by this section shall take effect on February 1, 1981.

fable.w: The section only increases the number of Tax Court judges, removes an age limitation on appointment, and sets an effective date. A tempting reading is that because it concerns a court it implicates the right to sue, but changing a court's composition does not grant any outside party a right to challenge a federal decision. Tax Court judges are federal officials, and the section provides for no consultation, comment, hearing, or advisory role for anyone outside the federal government.
fable.s: Subsection (a) of section 7443 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (relating to the number of judges on the Tax Court) is amended by striking out “16” and inserting in lieu thereof “19”.

qwen_block.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to increase the number of judges on the Tax Court and remove an age limitation for appointment. These are internal administrative changes to a federal judicial body. There is no requirement for consultation with, or participation by, any parties outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private entities). The actors involved are federal officials and judges, who are inside the government.
qwen_block.s: Subsection (a) of section 7443 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (relating to the number of judges on the Tax Court) is amended by striking out “16” and inserting in lieu thereof “19”.
qwen_block.b: Temptation: The text mentions "judges" and "appointment," which might suggest a process involving external candidates or public input. However, the text only changes the number of judges and removes an age limit for appointment; it does not describe the appointment process itself or require any consultation with outside parties. The Tax Court is a federal entity, and its internal staffing changes are internal government matters.

opus.w: This section only raises the number of Tax Court judges from 16 to 19, removes an age limit on appointments and sets an effective date. Nothing in it has the federal government consult or coordinate with anyone outside the government. The tempting reading would treat the judicial appointment provisions as a decision process, but any appointment involves only federal actors, and the section adds no outside-party process at all.
opus.b: **Tempting reading:** Section 7443 governs appointments to the Tax Court, so this could look like a decision process with outsiders involved. It fails against the definition because the section only changes the number of judges and removes an age limit. Nobody outside the federal government is consulted, and there is no comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to increase the number of Tax Court judges and remove an age limitation. These are internal administrative changes to the federal judiciary structure. There is no requirement for consultation with, or participation by, any entity outside the federal government (such as states, tribes, the public, or private organizations). The appointment process involves the President and Senate, both of which are inside the federal government.
qwen_chat.s: (a) Increase in Number of Judges.—Subsection (a) of section 7443 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (relating to the number of judges on the Tax Court) is amended by striking out “16” and inserting in lieu thereof “19”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that increasing the number of judges or removing age limits involves public participation because judges are appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, which involves political actors. However, the Senate is part of the federal government (inside), and the appointment process itself is an internal governmental procedure, not a consultation with outside parties. Furthermore, this section merely changes the statutory parameters for appointments; it does not create a new mechanism for outside consultation, advisory boards, public hearings, or rights to sue.
